3. 
Agencies' Voluntary Use of Oral Hearings in Informal Rulemaking. 
Although limiting the discretion of courts to order agencies to “hybridize” their 
rulemakings otherwise governed by section 553, agencies retain the discretion 
on their own initiative to conduct oral hearings, of greater or lesser formahty, 
if they think it useful. After all, while eschewing cross-examination, the 
Nuclear Regulatory Commission held just such a hearing on a voluntary basis 
as part of its rulemaking on measuring the environmental hazards of fuel 
reprocessing or disposal.
To note but one other conspicuous example, the FCC, in 2010, adopted 
what turned out be a set of short-lived “open Internet” rules as a response to 
significant public sentiment in favor of so-called “net neutrality.” The rules 
require broadband providers to disclose information regarding their network 
management practices, performance, and the commercial terms of their 
broadband services; prohibit broadband providers from blocking lawful 
content, apphcations, services, or non-harmful devices; and forbid 
“unreasonable discrimination” in the transmission of network traffic. In 
addition to issuing a notice of proposed rulemaking. Preserving the Open 
Internet et al., Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 24 FCC Red. 13064 (2009), the 
Commission staged five pubhc workshops in 2009 and 2010 involving panel 
presentations on both the technical and pohey issues implicated by the 
proposed rules, followed by audience interaction—^including a “remote” 
audience communicating by email or Twitter feed. Each of the hearings was 
webcast and video-archived, so that it could become the subject of further 
pubhc comment, even from people and parties who were not viewing the 
proceedings in real time. Links to the programs appear at http://www.fcc.gov/ 
encyclopedia/open-internet-workshops-and-speeches. The 86-page “Report and 
Order” (excluding appendices and separate Commissioner opinions) 
accompanying the final rule. In the Matter of Preserving the Open Internet 
Broadband Industry Practices, GN Docket No. 09-191, WC Docket No. 07-52 
(2010), summarized the pubhc input from ah sources and reported that the 
rulemaking had eheited over 100,000 written comments; a hst of commenters 
itself occupied a single-spaced appendix of over 15 pages.
d. Ex Parte Contacts in Rulemaking
By the 1970s, both agencies and courts understood that rules were to 
be based (and reviewed) on a “record,” even when the authoring agency was 
subject only to the requirements of section 553. General acceptance of this 
proposition blurred the historical distinction between formal procedures in 
which decisions were based exclusively on the evidentiary record and 
informal processes in which the “record” consisted of whatever materials 
the agency drew upon in reaching a decision, regardless of how it gained 
access to the materials. That agencies should not rely on any material not 
placed in the record as possible support for their decisions seems a logical 
corollary oiNova Scotia's requirement that parties have an opportunity to 
comment on the crucial factual and theoretical bases for agency rules.
